DOORS 👁️ — teardown

SURVIVAL-LOOP · LSPLASH (Group) · placeId 6516141723

A co-op horror walker — the genre benchmark on Roblox (7.58B visits). The loop: advance door by door through a procedural hotel, search rooms (gold, keys, items) and react to monsters — hide in a closet / under a bed, run a scripted chase, or look / don't look. One mistake ends the run; leftover gold converts to knobs and you go again, deeper through the floors (The Hotel → The Rooms → Floor 2 The Mines). Progress is doors and floors cleared; power is items (Lighter, Flashlight, Crucifix, keys) from Jeff's Shop for Gold and the Pre-Run Shop for Knobs. This teardown follows the recorded run (The Hotel to Door 16, died to Rush, 295 Gold) cross-checked with the wiki for what lies beyond. Focus: how horror UX and threat telegraphing hold tens of millions of players.

01Classification — game atoms

What the game is at the mechanics level. Pre-classification read the store text as a 'simulator-grinder' (Interact→earn→upgrade) — a storefront mistake: observation shows a co-op survival-horror with reactive monster avoidance and procedural runs, with no farm→upgrade core.

Verb
Advance — move to the next door (doors mostly open on approach; the repeated input is walk forward, search a room, hide/run)
Theme
Door-by-door horror escape: open the numbered doors of a procedural hotel, look for gold/keys/items and survive scripted monsters (hide/run/look); die and the run ends — you go again and deeper through the floors
Core systems
Reactive monster avoidance (hide/run/look) · procedural run (RoomGen) · items (light, Crucifix, keys) · Guiding Light (diegetic hint) · location floors · co-op · badges/dailies
Economy
Gold — in-run (from drawers/tables/chests), spent at Jeff's Shop (Door 52) · Knobs — persistent (leftover gold ×1/20 at run end + Robux + group/codes), spent at the Pre-Run Shop and some cosmetics · Robux — Revives, 5X Boost, Knob packs, skins, Admin Panel
Mask
The storefront/description = 'A horror game involving doors' (neutral), and the text-only pre-class wrongly returned 'Interact→earn→upgrade'. Observation: this is survival-horror — progress is not through output upgrades but through doors and floors, and the core is reacting to monsters, not earning
Archetype
SURVIVAL-LOOP — gathering resources, maintenance (light/HP) and risk management (monsters) extend the run; the goal is to get further through doors and floors
Progression
Completion by doors/floors: Door 1 → 50 (Library) → 100 (Electrical, escape the hotel) → The Rooms → Floor 2 The Mines. Inside a run it is round-based (die → restart); on top sits a persistent meta (Knobs, cosmetics, 91 badges)
[SURVIVAL-LOOP: advance→search→react→survive] + entity-hazards + procedural-run + inventory-equipment + guidance-rail + location-ladder + social-multipliers + quests | {co-op-horror-run · round-based · cooperative} × completion-ladder — genre benchmark: reactive monster avoidance + procedural run + Guiding Light; the 'ceremony' is not a reward reveal but a threat set-piece (see chapter 13) $ wall:run-death→offer:revive-and-cosmetics ! none

02Passport & market

Not a niche low-CCU neighbor but one of Roblox's biggest horror games: 7.58B visits, ~24K online, 92.95% rating. By the Welcome badge, 519M players have passed through — a rare scale for measuring retention.

A 'living genre benchmark' profile: DOORS set the template for co-op horror on Roblox, and its online holds for years on updates (Hotel+ → Floor 2 The Mines → The Great Outdoors → events). That is valuable two ways: first, the badge funnel (chapter 12) shows a retention curve over hundreds of millions of players; second, the mechanics are polished into a reference that the whole walker genre copies from — including this pool's neighbors (backrooms/horror-walkers).

03FTUE — lobby and entering a run

UX is the focus. Onboarding runs through a LIVE HALL, not modals: you stand among players, surrounded by mode elevators, the STORE and HOST GAME. Barrier to entry is low: press an elevator → load → hotel.

The FTUE is diegetic: the game does not explain itself with text but drops you into a living hall where everything is an object (elevators = modes, counter = STORE, button = host). Inside the hotel, teaching runs through Guiding Light (blue hints to doors and items) and first finds (key → a slot appears → carry it to a door). Within a couple of rooms a newcomer grasps the contour — search → carry → open → hide — and then hints fade. A low barrier to entry plus instant immersion is half of why hundreds of millions came in.

04A run through The Hotel

The core is a chain of rooms: you enter, search (gold, key, item), react to a threat (hide/run), advance to the next door. Below, frame by frame from the recording: The Hotel to Door 16.

The loop is short and tense: room → search → react → next door. Key UX decisions are visible immediately — doors open by themselves (no friction on advancing), hiding is one-button (closet/bed), and a threat is almost always telegraphed (lights flicker, the sound changes, Guiding Light names the monster) before it can kill. Death is not a dead-end punishment but the end of a round with a quantified result and instant Play Again: the short 'die → straight back in' loop is the engine of retention.

05Entities — the threat roster

The heart of the game is not combat but REACTION: each monster has its own 'survival verb' (hide / run / look / don't look) and its own telegraph. Below is the Hotel roster (+ Mines/Rooms), from the wiki; in the recording Screech and Rush are confirmed.

EntityWhere · typeHow it attacksHow to surviveTelegraph
RushHotel · set-pieceraces through all rooms, breaks bulbs; catches you = deathhide in a closet / under a bed before it passesflickering lights + rising rumble/roar (obs.)
AmbushHotel · set-piecelike Rush but rebounds back and forth up to ~6 timesre-hide between passes (defeats camping)like Rush, in repeated waves
SeekHotel · chasescripted chase; fall behind and it catches yourun the blue hints, duck under furniture, jumpblack eyes on walls/paintings, a slime pool
FigureHotel · Door 50 & 100blind, hunts by sound (a heartbeat meter)stay quiet; hide in bookcases; solve the code (Library) / breaker (Electrical)heavy footsteps, heartbeat indicator
ScreechHotel · 'look''psst' in the dark; bite for −35…40 HPturn and look at it in time'psst' sound + grinning face (obs.)
HaltHotel · 'turn around'traps you in a green hallwaysprint past, turn on 'Turn Around!'green light + text
EyesHotel · 'don't look'looking at it drains HP fastlook at the floor/wall, walk pasta mass of purple eyes in the room
TimothyHotel · jump-scareleaps out of a drawer, startles (−a little HP)nothing — it is just a scarewhen searching a drawer
DupeHotel · trapa fake door at a fork hurts youtake the door lit by Guiding Lightseveral doors to choose from
HideHotel · anti-campejects/harms you if you stay in a closet too longdon't camp — leave on 'GET OUT'a timer while hiding
Guiding LightHotel · helper— (friendly)follow the blue light to doors/itemsblue glow hint
El Goblino · BobHotel · NPC— (harmless, lore/comic)a rest room ~Door 50—
Grumble · Giggle · GloombatsFloor 2 Minesboss (Room 150) / ceiling drop / flock on your lightsee chapter 08 (Floor 2)laughing above / attack on your flashlight
A-60 · A-90 · A-120The Roomsthe stalker of the endless winghide / keep distancenamed after the room it appears in
LookmanBackdoordamage if you look at itlook away—

The roster's genius is readability: each monster is one clear 'survival verb' and one signal. Hide (Rush/Ambush), run (Seek), look (Screech), don't look (Eyes/Lookman), turn around (Halt), be quiet (Figure). Players learn not with an 'HP table' but with a set of simple reaction rules, and almost every threat is telegraphed in advance (light/sound/Guiding Light). Plus anti-patterns: Hide forbids sitting in a closet forever, Dupe punishes carelessness at forks. That is what makes the horror fair: scary, but you always know what to do.

06Items & Jeff's Shop

Power in DOORS is not stats but ITEMS: light, healing and the one 'weapon', the Crucifix. Bought mid-run at Jeff's Shop for Gold (Door 52) or ahead of time at the Pre-Run Shop for Knobs. The shop wasn't reached in the run (Door 16<52) — item skins appear in the STORE, Gold prices are from the wiki.

ItemWhat it doesWhere to getPrice (wiki)
Lighterweak, short-range light; lights candlesJeff's Shop / Pre-Run100 Gold / 50 Knobs
Flashlightstrongest, longest-lasting Floor-1 lightJeff's Shop / Pre-Run200 Gold / 100 Knobs
Lockpickopen a locked chest/door (no key needed)Jeff's Shop100 Gold
Skeleton Keyopen the skull door (always stocked)Jeff's Shop250 Gold
Vitaminsrestore healthJeff's ShopGold
Crucifixthe only 'weapon': banish a monster, then it is consumedJeff's Shop (boosted chance)Gold
Bandageheal; in the Mines it refills from found bandagesworld / Pre-Run—

Item design is about resource management, not build power. Light (Lighter → Flashlight) solves the base pain of darkness but drains. Vitamins/Bandage pay back damage. Keys/Lockpick/Skeleton Key are access (locked doors and chests = Gold and speed). And the Crucifix is the premium 'panic button': the only way to directly banish a monster, but single-use and not guaranteed in stock (a random 4 of 6 slots; Skeleton Key guaranteed, Crucifix boosted). Jeff's Shop (Door 52) is the single Gold sink in a run; the whole shop is ≈ 1,150 Gold, so the player constantly decides what they can afford.

07Economy: Gold · Knobs · Robux

Three currency layers with clear roles and almost no overlap: Gold is tactics inside a run, Knobs are strategic prep between runs, Robux is insurance and cosmetics.

LayerCurrencyHow to getWhere to spend
In a run (tactics)Golddrawers, tables, chests, wardrobes during a runJeff's Shop (Door 52)
Between runs (strategy)Knobsleftover gold at run end (~20 Gold → 1 Knob) + Robux + group/codesPre-Run Shop, some cosmetics
Real moneyRobux ⬡purchaseRevives, 5X Boost, Knob packs, skins, Admin Panel

The economy reads as 'risk → resource → prep'. You mine Gold by risk (searching under monster threat) and spend it immediately on survival at Jeff's Shop — that is in-round tactics. Leftovers on death don't burn but convert to Knobs (~20:1), so every run, even a lost one, moves the persistent axis: Knobs bank toward items you carry into the next run (Pre-Run Shop) and toward cosmetics. Robux is a separate layer of safety (Revive, 'second chance per floor') and expression (skins). The axes barely overlap, so monetization doesn't break run balance: a paying player buys insurance and looks, not 'power against monsters'.

08Floors & modes

Progression is a ladder of locations. The Hotel teaches the rules, Floor 2 The Mines changes them (active tasks instead of pure reaction), and the modes (Rooms, Backdoor, Battle, Daily) extend the ceiling.

Location / modeWhat it isHow it differs
The Hotelthe main floor, Doors 1–100base rules: hide/run/look; finale is Figure in Electrical (Door 100)
The Roomsthe endless wing after Door 100one stalker (A-60/A-90/A-120) + Jack; a race for score/loot
Floor 2 · The Minesa big expansion beyond the hotelactive tasks: generators+fuses, minecarts+levers; new monsters (Grumble, Giggle, Gloombats)
The Backdoora prequel/side winga timed speed-run; the monster Lookman ('don't look')
The Great Outdoorsa 2025 map (35 floors)exterior locations (courtyard, mill, clearing) ⚠ per wiki
Battle Modea competitive mode (lobby elevator)a PvP branch ⚠ details beyond the run
Daily Runa daily seeded rungates some achievements ('Win any Daily Run with other players')

The location ladder is what turns one hotel into a years-long game. The Hotel is school: it teaches the vocabulary of monster reactions. The Rooms is an endless skill-check on the same rules. Floor 2 The Mines is a key shift: to pure reaction it adds active tasks (find fuses under Gloombat pressure, push minecarts), so the genre evolves from 'hide/run' to 'hide/run + solve/gather'. Plus format modes (Backdoor on a timer, Battle Mode PvP, Daily for return). For the pool's neighbors this is a map of where to grow a walker beyond a base hotel.

09Monetization

Cosmetics-first, low pressure on the core. Two gamepasses (Kitty Bundle, Admin Panel) plus a wall of skins/bundles and functional offers (Revives, 5X Boost, Knob packs) for Robux.

SKUPriceWhat it gives
KITTY BUNDLE (gamepass)⬡299a cosmetic bundle
ADMIN PANEL (gamepass)⬡499spawn entities/items, troll; 'cannot gain progression'
Sought Crucifix (bundle)⬡4999special sounds and animations for the Crucifix
Classic Gear Flashlight⬡3999'Nostalgiabait' — a flashlight skin
Chicky Nuggy Crucifix skin⬡2999a special inspect animation ('dip & eat')
Item skins (Lockpick/Lighter/Shears/Bandage…)⬡499–1499item cosmetics
5X Boost (3 uses) · Knob packs⬡ variesprogress boost · Knob packs (%EXTRA)
Revives · Stardust · Value Pack⬡ variessecond chance per floor · currency

Monetization is pointedly cosmetic and barely presses on run fairness. The priciest items (Sought Crucifix 4999⬡, Classic Gear 3999⬡) are sound/animation/style on items, not an advantage against monsters. Functional offers exist but are soft: Revive (second chance per floor), 5X Boost (progress speed-up, 3 uses), Knob packs (skip the persistent-currency grind). Even the Admin Panel (499⬡) honestly disables progression ('cannot gain progression while enabled') — it is a sandbox toy, not a pay-gate. Plus a 'free Revive for joining the group' converts players into community followers.

10HUD & menus

In a run the HUD is nearly empty (flashlight, hotbar, a Gold counter) — so it doesn't break the horror; the whole meta lives in the lobby (STORE, Achievements, Creators, updates board). Below are the key menu screens; duplicates dropped.

The interface split is exemplary for horror. In a run the HUD is minimal (flashlight in hand, item hotbar, a quiet Gold counter, the occasional Guiding Light hint) — any extra UI would kill immersion and fear. In the lobby, by contrast, dense meta-navigation: STORE, Achievements (with a content map), Creators, the updates board, leaderboards. Everything 'administrative' (progress, purchases, social comparison) lives outside the run, and the run itself stays clean and tense. A direct lesson for walkers: menus in the hall, the run screen for atmosphere.

11Retention

Hooks: the short 'die → straight back in' loop, Guiding Light (no frustration), the ladder of floors, events/cosmetics, co-op with friends and 91 badges as long-horizon milestones.

Several layers drive return. The short loop: death → quantified result → instant Play Again — 'one more run' with almost no friction. Fair horror: Guiding Light and threat telegraphs keep difficulty on the edge of 'scary but fair', not 'died for no reason'. The content ladder: floors (Hotel → Rooms → Mines → Outdoors) and events (Archives/anniversary) give a 'what's next'. Social: co-op and dailies with a friends bonus (in the recording, 'Playing with Friends +0%' — with friends it would be more). Badges (91) are long named milestones. The combo of 'low barrier + long ladder + social hook' is what yields an online that holds for years.

The funnel is the main takeaway. Welcome (entry) was earned 519M times; One Of Many (first death) — 68%: two thirds die almost immediately — that is the horror norm and part of the loop. Then the classic drop-off: Ten Of Many (10 deaths/runs) is already 14%, and Hundred Of Many — 1.1%. Named milestone achievements (Rock Bottom, Interconnected, the BLOXFEST event at 0.01%) are a thin hardcore tail in fractions of a percent. It reads as the universal curve: a giant entry, a fast first 'failure' as part of the fun, and a long thin tail for those who master monster timing. For walkers the lesson is: what retains is not 'difficulty' but fairness and a short loop at the entrance.

13Sound, VFX and threat telegraphing

In horror the 'juice' is FEAR delivered fairly: a telegraph (light+sound+text) before the hit, not a cheap jump-scare from nowhere. Below, from the captured moment and run observations.

Rush/Screech telegraph: a build-up, then a peak

The acoustics of the captured moment are a gradual, bright build, not a single sharp hit (moderate transient, wide dynamic range): the game first telegraphs the threat — lights flicker, the ambient timbre shifts, Guiding Light names the monster — and only then comes the peak (Rush's roar / Screech's bite). This is the key trick of fair horror: the player gets a split second to react, so death feels 'my fault', not 'unfair'.

InteractionVisualSound / characterPurpose
Rush/Ambush arrivalbulbs flicker and break, shakerising rumble → roar (peak)telegraph → run to cover
Screechgrinning face in the darkquiet 'psst' → loud screechan attention check, 'look'
Seek chasefurniture collapses, hands reacha musical chase 'drive'an adrenaline set-piece
Opening a doorthe door swings by itselfcreak/thudthe rhythm of advancing
Search/finda drawer opens, coins/itemsoft 'rustle' + Gold 'chime'a micro-reward for risk
Death/run resultOverview screen + Revivea sharp death stinger → silenceend of round, Revive offer

What to take: in horror the 'juice' budget goes not into decorating the routine but into a fair telegraph of the threat (light → sound → name → peak) and into a readable signal per reaction type (its own sound for 'look', 'run', 'hide'). The routine (walking, searching) is quiet and tactile; the peak (a monster) is loud and telegraphed. Then it is scary and fair at once — and the player hits Play Again instead of leaving annoyed.

16What to take into your project

Concrete decisions from the genre benchmark (7.58B visits), portable into your own walker/horror — and a reference for the pool's neighbors (backrooms/horror-walkers).

1

One monster = one 'survival verb' + one signal

Rush=hide, Seek=run, Screech=look, Eyes=don't look, Halt=turn around. Players learn by rules, not an HP table. Give each threat its own readable signal (its own sound/color/text).

2

Telegraph the threat before the hit

Flickering lights + a sound shift + Guiding Light naming the monster give a split second to react. Death then feels 'my fault', not 'unfair' — and the player hits Play Again.

3

Diegetic hinting instead of a tutorial

Guiding Light (a blue light) leads to doors, items and hiding spots right in the world. Zero modals, a minimal barrier to entry — half the reason hundreds of millions came in.

4

A short 'die → straight back in' loop

Death is not a dead-end but the end of a round with a quantified result (Door 16, Gold 295, +Knobs) and instant Play Again. That is the retention engine in a run-based game.

5

Anti-camp and anti-cheese mechanics

Hide ejects you from a closet for sitting too long; Dupe punishes carelessness at a fork. The design forces you to PLAY, not to exploit safe poses.

6

Two currencies: tactics in a run, strategy between

Gold is mined by risk and spent immediately (Jeff's Shop); leftovers convert to persistent Knobs (20:1) for items in the next run. Even a lost run advances the meta.

7

Monetize cosmetics and insurance, not power

The pricey stuff (Sought Crucifix 4999⬡) is sound/animation, not an advantage; Revive/Boost are soft insurance; the Admin Panel honestly disables progression. No pay-gate on monsters — trust preserved.

8

Grow by a ladder of locations, changing the rules

The Hotel teaches reactions → Floor 2 The Mines adds active tasks (generators, minecarts) → modes (Backdoor timed, Battle PvP, Daily). The genre evolves rather than repeats.

9

Menus in the hall, the run screen for atmosphere

All meta (STORE, achievements, leaderboards) is moved to the lobby; in a run the HUD is nearly empty. Nothing breaks immersion at the moment it should be scary.
